frames.narration: A replica has room for 4 sequences. Alone, one request costs a 20 ms weight read plus 1 ms per sequence: 21 ms per token, about 48 tokens/s. Four requests together cost 24 ms per step, about 167 tokens/s.
Static batching: A (30 tokens), B (300), C (40) and D (25) start together. Each step reads the weights once for all four.
By step 40 A, C and D are done, but the batch runs to step 300 (7.2 s). Their slots idle while E and F wait, and A's 30 token answer reaches the user after 7.2 s instead of 0.7 s.
Continuous batching: the scheduler runs every step. D ends at step 25 (0.6 s) and is returned at once; E takes its slot at step 26. A and C leave and F joins the same way.

F has a 3,000 token prompt. Prefilled in one go it costs about 300 ms, so every running user freezes for 0.3 s. Chunked prefill spreads it over 12 steps of 256 tokens: each step is 50 ms, never longer.

KV memory is paged: blocks of 16 tokens come from a free pool as sequences grow. A finished sequence frees its blocks immediately. Reserving 4,096 tokens for a 530 token chat would waste 87%; paging wastes under one block.
A traffic spike arrives. The scheduler's queue is capped at 8 waiting requests; request number 9 is rejected at once with a 429 instead of waiting minutes.

The router retries on the replica with the least queued plus running work, not round-robin. Scaling on queue depth adds replicas, but loading weights takes minutes, so the cap is what protects latency meanwhile.
